In Chapter 14 we introduced the general logic of ANOVA and used its independent-samples variant to analyze data from a between-participants design. But like the $t$ test, ANOVA has varieties for different situations. In this chapter we'll introduce the **related-samples ANOVA**, also called a one-way repeated-measures ANOVA. Just like the related-samples $t$ test, this is for within-participants or matched-subjects designs. The logic of $F$ is the same; what's new is how we account for differences between people.

## Repeated measures, repeated

We spent Chapter 13 looking at data from a handful of kids who had completed a racing game twice, first alone and then against another kid. We used a related-samples $t$ test to compare the two times via difference scores, subtracting each kid's alone-race time from their competition time. The kids were generally a little faster racing against a rival. But we left a loose end. Was it the *competition* that spurred them to race quicker, or was it just practice at turning the reel? With just two races from each kid, and competition always coming after the solo race, we couldn't tell.

What might we do to tease apart the possible effects of practice and competition? One idea is to add another race. If the kids raced alone *twice* before competing, we could see how much they improved from one solo race to the next, where practice is arguably the only explanation for a consistent difference. We'd then ask whether the competition trial brought any additional improvement. It's not a perfect solution; improvement in the third race could still be down to practice. But if the improvement seems greater than we'd expect from practice alone, that would fit with the social facilitation boost of racing against a competitor.

In fact, Norman Triplett gave each child six timed trials, with different sequences of solo and competition trials [@triplett1898dynamogenic]. Here we'll use the first three trials from five other children---not the ones from Chapter 13---who all followed the same order: alone, alone, then competition, as shown in @tbl-related-anova-data. (As before, to make a useful teaching example, I cherry-picked children who raced in this order from the group Triplett classified as "stimulated positively" by competition, and rounded their times to whole seconds. This isn't a full reanalysis of Triplett's data.)

| Child | First alone | Second alone | Competition |
|:------|--:|--:|--:|
| Stephen M. | 51 | 50 | 43 |
| Mary W. | 56 | 53 | 46 |
| Bertha A. | 56 | 49 | 48 |
| Clyde G. | 36 | 35 | 32 |
| Lucile W. | 52 | 50 | 43 |
| $M$ | 50.20 | 47.40 | 42.40 |
| $SS$ | 272.80 | 201.20 | 153.20 |

: Times (in seconds) for five children from Triplett's study. The columns follow the order of their first three trials. {#tbl-related-anova-data}

How do we analyze all three conditions? With two scores, we simply subtracted each child's pair of times to get a single difference score. Here there are three scores per kid, allowing multiple pairwise comparisons. We'll get to those with post-hoc tests, as we did in Chapter 14, but simple pairwise subtraction can't handle the whole set of scores in a single test. But you know what can: ANOVA.

{{< include quizzes/15-related-anova-third-condition.qmd >}}

## Partitioning variance in related samples

Again, the idea is that some kids are just faster overall, some are slower overall. Like, check out Clyde G.'s times in @tbl-related-anova-data. Clyde was not messing around---he totally demolished the other kids' times in every one of his races. How can we extend the ANOVA logic to separate that source of variability from differences between conditions and other sources?

Let's think in terms of partitioning. In Chapter 14 we split the total sum of squared deviations into between-groups and within-groups components. I said that any treatment effect contributes to differences between groups, while chance contributes both between and within groups. But I was glossing over "chance" there. I said it is made up of sampling error and other reasons people's scores differ. Well, one of those reasons is consistent individual differences between kids. @fig-partitioning-independent labels that separately.

::: {#fig-partitioning-independent}
{{< interactive-figure relatedRecapPartitionDiagram makeVariancePartitionDiagram options='{"preset":"independent-detailed","formula":false,"ariaLabel":"Diagram partitioning the total sum of squares into variability between groups, which contains any treatment effect, sampling error, and individual differences, and variability within groups, which contains sampling error and individual differences."}' fallback="Diagram partitioning the total sum of squares into variability between groups, which contains any treatment effect, sampling error, and individual differences, and variability within groups, which contains sampling error and individual differences." >}}
:::

With a between-participants design and independent-samples ANOVA, we can only split the total into between-groups and within-groups variability. Individual differences will contribute to within-groups variability, because each group is made up of a bunch of different people. And they contribute to between-groups variability, because each group is a different set of unrelated participants.

A within-participants design changes this. We still have a bunch of different people within each condition, so individual differences contribute to within-groups variability. Clyde G.'s super-speed makes each group substantially more variable. But now the same people appear in every condition. Whatever it is about Clyde that makes him so much faster than the other kids, he brings it with him in all three races; it is consistent across groups. So the design itself eliminates individual differences as a source of variability between groups. The only things that can make the condition means differ are the treatment effect and sampling error.

As a result, we have a slight problem. The numerator and denominator for our $F$ ratio are no longer conceptually balanced. The numerator contains treatment plus sampling error, while the denominator contains sampling error plus individual differences. But the good news is that we can *mathematically* extract those individual differences from the denominator as well, leaving a balanced ratio.

To do this, we split the within-groups sum of squares into two components: between-people variability, $SS_{\text{people}}$, and the remaining error, $SS_{\text{error}}$.^[I'm simplifying slightly. Error here isn't necessarily just sampling error, strictly defined, which is why @fig-partitioning-related calls it "remaining chance." Children might respond differently to practice or competition, or have a particularly good or bad trial. Those departures from the average pattern remain in the error component.]

::: {#fig-partitioning-related}
{{< interactive-figure relatedPartitionDiagram makeVariancePartitionDiagram options='{"preset":"related","formula":false,"ariaLabel":"Diagram partitioning the total sum of squares into variability between groups, which contains any treatment effect plus remaining chance, and variability within groups, which contains remaining chance and individual differences and is further partitioned into variability between people, which contains individual differences, and error, which contains the remaining chance."}' fallback="Diagram partitioning the total sum of squares into variability between groups, which contains any treatment effect plus remaining chance, and variability within groups, which contains remaining chance and individual differences and is further partitioned into variability between people, which contains individual differences, and error, which contains the remaining chance." >}}
:::

We divide $SS_{\text{error}}$ by its degrees of freedom to get $MS_{\text{error}}$, our new denominator for the related-samples $F$ ratio. We will still use the same numerator, $MS_{\text{between}}$. Under the null hypothesis, both estimate the same remaining variance. A difference between the population means can make the numerator larger, just as before.

## Calculating related-samples ANOVA

Happily, the math is relatively straightforward. But before we get to the new equations, let's see how we separate out the people component using the data from the five kids in @tbl-related-anova-data. The key is to regroup the scores: so far we've grouped them by condition; for the between-people component in @act-related-partition we'll group them by child.

::::: {#act-related-partition .callout-tip .interactive}
## Where the individual differences go

{{< interactive-figure relatedAnovaExplorer makeAnovaVariabilityExplorer options='{"stage":"populations","calculations":false,"controlsOpen":false,"people":["Stephen","Mary W.","Bertha","Clyde","Lucile"],"groups":[{"name":"First alone","values":[51,56,56,36,52]},{"name":"Second alone","values":[50,53,49,35,50]},{"name":"Competition","values":[43,46,48,32,43]}],"axisLabel":"Time (seconds)","personColors":[0,3,7,1,5],"xMin":30,"xMax":60,"populationSd":7.23}' fallback="Interactive diagram of five children timed in three conditions. The scores regroup into one row per child, each child's scores slide to that child's mean, and the squared deviations fill a people layer at the bottom of the within-groups sum of squares. What remains above it is error, and only the between-groups and error layers are divided by their degrees of freedom." >}}

:::: {.callout-footer}
::: {.tutorial-step data-major="scores" data-major-title="Scores" data-title="Scores" data-action='{"stage":"populations","phase":"observe","animate":false}'}
Here are the five children's times, grouped by condition. Each child contributes one score to each row. For now, the calculations are the same as in Chapter 14, so the dots are colored by race type rather than by child.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="total" data-major-title="Total" data-title="Total" data-action='{"stage":"total","phase":"sum","animate":true}'}
As in Chapter 14, we start with each score's deviation from the grand mean. Squaring and adding them gives $SS_{\text{total}}$.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="within" data-major-title="Within" data-title="Within" data-action='{"stage":"within","phase":"sum","animate":true}'}
Measuring deviations from each condition's own mean gives $SS_{\text{within}}$. The spread within each row includes individual differences---the fact that some children are generally faster than others. We'll separate that out in a moment.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="between" data-major-title="Between" data-title="Between" data-action='{"stage":"between","phase":"sum","animate":true}'}
The differences between condition means account for $SS_{\text{between}}$. Because of the within-participants design, the between-groups variability does not include individual differences. That's a product of the design, not any new math.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="people" data-major-title="People" data-title="Recolor" data-action='{"stage":"people","phase":"recolour","animate":true}'}
Now for the new part. We will use the relatedness of the scores from each kid to separate the individual-differences part of the within-groups variability. First, we'll just color the dots by child. See Clyde's orange dots, all the way to the left of the others?
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="people" data-major-title="People" data-title="Rows" data-action='{"stage":"people","phase":"rows","animate":true}'}
We'll regroup the scores into one row per child, to make the relatedness more visually obvious. Next we'll do much the same as we did for between-groups variability, but compare the *children's* means instead of condition means.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="people" data-major-title="People" data-title="Averages" data-action='{"stage":"people","phase":"observe","animate":true}'}
Having grouped the scores by child, we find each kid's average across their three scores. If individual differences were the only source of variability---no other chance error at all---then each kid's time would be the same in every race. So we imagine that all three of their scores are equal to their own average time.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="people" data-major-title="People" data-title="Deviations" data-action='{"stage":"people","phase":"deviations","animate":true}'}
Now we find the deviation of each child's mean from the grand mean. Is this looking familiar?
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="people" data-major-title="People" data-title="Squares" data-action='{"stage":"people","phase":"squares","animate":true}'}
Next we square each deviation. Larger squares represent children whose overall times were farther from the grand mean, whether faster or slower.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="people" data-major-title="People" data-title="Sum" data-action='{"stage":"people","phase":"sum","animate":true}'}
And finally we add those squares, counting each one three times to represent the child's three scores. They add up to $SS_{\text{people}}$, part of the within-groups variability we already counted.

Now we're basically done. There's a little sliver of unaccounted variability left over. That's the error component.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="centre" data-major-title="Error" data-title="Center" data-action='{"stage":"centre","phase":"shift","animate":true}'}
To quantify the leftover variability, we shift each kid's cluster of scores so that each child's mean aligns with the grand mean. Each child becomes exactly average, without those pesky individual differences pushing them apart. Notice that Clyde doesn't look exceptional any more. But each kid's three scores still vary from one another. That variation includes the differences between conditions. To find the error, we'll look at how far each adjusted score falls from its condition's mean.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="centre" data-major-title="Error" data-title="Lanes" data-action='{"stage":"centre","phase":"lanes","animate":true}'}
We put the adjusted scores back into their condition rows. The condition means are unchanged, but the spread around them is much smaller because the children no longer differ in overall speed.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="centre" data-major-title="Error" data-title="What's left" data-action='{"stage":"centre","phase":"squares","animate":true}'}
Now we find each adjusted score's deviation from its condition mean and square it. This is the variability that remains after accounting for both the conditions and the children's overall levels.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="centre" data-major-title="Error" data-title="Error" data-action='{"stage":"centre","phase":"sum","animate":true}'}
The squares fill the remaining part of $SS_{\text{within}}$, showing $SS_{\text{error}}$ itself. We could have obtained the same answer by just subtracting $SS_{\text{people}}$ from $SS_{\text{within}}$. Or, put another way, $SS_{\text{people}} + SS_{\text{error}} = SS_{\text{within}}$.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="compare" data-major-title="Compare" data-title="Partition" data-action='{"stage":"compare","phase":"partition","animate":true}'}
Let's put it all together. $SS_{\text{total}}$ now has three parts: between groups, between people, and error.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="compare" data-major-title="Compare" data-title="Split" data-action='{"stage":"compare","phase":"split","animate":true}'}
For the $F$ ratio, we take the between-groups and error components. We leave individual differences behind and use only the error component of the within-groups variability as our denominator.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="compare" data-major-title="Compare" data-title="F" data-action='{"stage":"compare","phase":"f","animate":true}'}
As usual, we divide each sum by its degrees of freedom to get the mean squares. In this case $df_{\text{between}} = 2$ and $df_{\text{error}} = 8$; we'll see where that 8 comes from shortly. Our numerator mean square is much bigger than the new denominator mean square, so our $F$ ratio will be large.
:::
::::

:::::

### Sums of squares and degrees of freedom

So here's how we calculate this modified $F$ ratio for related-samples data.[^related-complete]

[^related-complete]: These formulas assume a complete set of scores: each person contributes one score in every condition. If someone misses a condition, we can't simply leave that cell blank and carry on with the same calculation.

As @act-related-partition showed, the equations and degrees of freedom for $SS_{\text{total}}$, $SS_{\text{between}}$, and $SS_{\text{within}}$ are the same as in Chapter 14.

The only difference is that we will now split the within-groups variability into two components: between-people and error. The equation[^related-computational] for between people has the same form as $SS_{\text{between}}$, with person means in place of group means:

$$ SS_{\text{people}} = \Sigma k(M_{\text{person}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2 $$

$M_{\text{person}}$ is the mean of one person's scores across the conditions. We square each person's deviation from the grand mean and multiply by $k$, the number of conditions, since each person's mean represents $k$ scores. Then we add them up. Same idea as between groups, just regrouping the scores by person.

The final component, error, is what's left after taking individual differences out of within-groups variability. It will provide our denominator, and it's easiest to find by subtraction:

$$ SS_{\text{error}} = SS_{\text{within}} - SS_{\text{people}} $$

Or, as @act-related-partition showed, we can get the same answer directly, from each score's deviation from its group mean once that person's overall deviation from the grand mean has been taken out:

$$ SS_{\text{error}} = \Sigma (X - M_{\text{person}} - M_{\text{group}} + M_{\text{grand}})^2 $$

For each score, subtract that child's mean and add the grand mean: $X - M_{\text{person}} + M_{\text{grand}}$. Stephen's mean is 1.33 seconds above the grand mean, so we subtract 1.33 from each of his times. His first time, 51 seconds, becomes 49.67. All three of Stephen's scores move by the same amount; their differences stay the same. We've taken out differences in overall speed without changing the condition means. Then we subtract the group mean from each adjusted score, square, and add them up to get the error sum of squares.

The two new components have degrees of freedom of their own. For $SS_{\text{people}}$, we computed the deviation of each person's mean from the grand mean. Here $n$ is the number of people, so that's $n$ means, deviating from a single grand mean: $df_{\text{people}} = n - 1$.[^related-matched]

Degrees of freedom are partitioned just like sums of squares, so we can find $df_{\text{error}}$ by subtraction too:

$$
\begin{aligned}
df_{\text{error}} &= df_{\text{within}} - df_{\text{people}} \\
&= (N - k) - (n - 1)
\end{aligned}
$$

Why subtract $n - 1$, rather than one for every person? The condition means have already used up $k$ degrees of freedom, leaving $N - k$ within groups. Now we're accounting for how far each person's mean is from the grand mean. Those deviations must add up to zero, so once we know $n - 1$ of them, the last is fixed. Accounting for the people component therefore uses another $n - 1$ degrees of freedom. For our five children and three conditions, that leaves $(15 - 3) - (5 - 1) = 8$ for error.

Since each of the $n$ people contributes $k$ scores, $N = nk$. Substituting that into the equation gives a shorter way to write the same thing:

$$
\begin{aligned}
df_{\text{error}} &= (nk - k) - (n - 1) \\
&= (k - 1)(n - 1)
\end{aligned}
$$

[^related-matched]: In a matched-subjects design, we do the same calculation with matched sets in place of people. Each set contributes one score per condition, and $n$ counts sets. Other books may call the between-people component “between subjects” or “between participants.”

[^related-computational]: As in Chapter 14, there's also a computational version of this formula. It uses $P$, a participant total (the sum of the scores for one person), and $G$, the grand total.

    $$ SS_{\text{people}} = \Sigma \frac{P^2}{k} - \frac{G^2}{N} $$

    We'll stick with the definitional formula here too.

### Mean squares and $F$

Once we have the sums of squares and degrees of freedom, the rest is easy. We divide each relevant sum of squares by its degrees of freedom to get the mean squares, then take their ratio to get $F$. The numerator is the same as before; the denominator is now $MS_{\text{error}}$, rather than $MS_{\text{within}}$.

$$
\begin{align}
MS_{\text{between}} &= \frac{SS_{\text{between}}}{df_{\text{between}}} \\
MS_{\text{error}} &= \frac{SS_{\text{error}}}{df_{\text{error}}}
\end{align}
$$

$$ F = \frac{MS_{\text{between}}}{MS_{\text{error}}} $$

The interpretation of the $F$ ratio is also the same as with independent samples. A large numerator relative to the denominator is evidence against the null hypothesis.

By the way, with just two conditions, the related-samples ANOVA gives $F = t^2$, with the same $p$-value as the corresponding two-tailed related-samples $t$ test. Just as in Chapter 14, we're expressing the same evidence in a different way.

{{< include quizzes/15-related-anova-partitioning-variance.qmd >}}

## A related-samples ANOVA, step by step

So let's run through the hypothesis test for the five children in @tbl-related-anova-data.

### Step 1: State the hypotheses

As always, we start the hypothesis test by stating our hypotheses. The null here is that the population mean time is the same in all three conditions:

$$ H_0: \mu_{\text{first alone}} = \mu_{\text{second alone}} = \mu_{\text{competition}} $$

The alternative hypothesis is that at least one condition differs from at least one other.

### Step 2: Set the decision criteria

Step two is to determine the critical value for the test, with $\alpha = .05$. We use the same $F$ table as in Chapter 14, with the degrees of freedom for our numerator and new denominator:

$$ df_{\text{between}} = k - 1 = 2 $$

$$ df_{\text{error}} = (k - 1)(n - 1) = 2(4) = 8 $$

In @tbl-related-anova-critical, the column for 2 and the row for 8 give a critical $F$ of 4.46.

::: {#tbl-related-anova-critical}
{{< interactive-figure relatedAnovaCriticalTable makeFTable options='{"title":"Critical values for the competition test","alpha":0.05,"df1":{"from":1,"to":4},"df2":{"from":6,"to":12},"tableMinWidth":"0","maxWidth":"32rem","interactive":false,"selected":{"df1":2,"df2":8,"alpha":0.05}}' fallback="F table excerpt for numerator df 1 through 4 and denominator df 6 through 12, highlighting the .05 critical value of 4.46 at F(2, 8)." >}}

An excerpt of the $F$ table, with the critical value for $df = 2$ and $8$ highlighted.
:::

Note that if these 15 scores had come from independent samples, the denominator would have had 12 degrees of freedom and the critical value would have been 3.89. Our lower degrees of freedom mean we need a more extreme $F$ to reject the null, just as we saw with the related-samples $t$ test.

{{< include quizzes/15-related-anova-degrees-of-freedom.qmd >}}

### Step 3: Collect and analyze the data

Calculating $F$ by hand is a little labor-intensive, but a summary table helps, as in Chapter 14, with additional rows for between-people and error variability. @tbl-related-anova-summary-blank shows the equations for each element.

::: {#tbl-related-anova-summary-blank .sfs-summary-table}
| Source | $SS$ | $df$ | $MS$ | $F$ |
|:-------|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Between groups | $\Sigma n_{\text{group}}(M_{\text{group}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ | $k - 1$ | $\dfrac{SS_{\text{between}}}{df_{\text{between}}}$ | $\dfrac{MS_{\text{between}}}{MS_{\text{error}}}$ |
| Within groups | $\Sigma (X - M_{\text{group}})^2$ | $N - k$ | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |
| &emsp;Between people | $\Sigma k(M_{\text{person}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ | $n - 1$ | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |
| &emsp;Error | $SS_{\text{within}} - SS_{\text{people}}$ | $(k - 1)(n - 1)$ | $\dfrac{SS_{\text{error}}}{df_{\text{error}}}$ | []{.sfs-na} |
| Total | $\Sigma (X - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ | $N - 1$ | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |

A related-samples ANOVA summary table, showing each equation.
:::

To save you some trouble, @tbl-related-anova-data gives each condition's mean and sum of squares. Here are $n$, $k$, $N$, and $M_{\text{grand}}$ too. Remember that we have five children but 15 scores.

(I've rounded the values I'm showing to two decimal places, but the calculations use the unrounded values, so you'll need to do the same if you want your answers to match mine exactly.)

$$
\begin{gathered}
n = 5 \qquad k = 3 \qquad N = 15 \\
M_{\text{grand}} = 46.67
\end{gathered}
$$

First, the familiar components. Squaring each score's deviation from the grand mean and adding them gives the total sum of squares:

$$ SS_{\text{total}} = \Sigma (X - M_{\text{grand}})^2 = 783.33 $$

$$ df_{\text{total}} = N - 1 = 15 - 1 = 14 $$

For within groups, we can just add the three condition sums of squares from @tbl-related-anova-data:

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_{\text{within}} &= \Sigma (X - M_{\text{group}})^2 \\
&= 272.80 + 201.20 + 153.20 \\
&= 627.20
\end{aligned}
$$

$$ df_{\text{within}} = N - k = 15 - 3 = 12 $$

For between groups, we find each condition mean's deviation from the grand mean, square it, and multiply by the five scores it represents:

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_{\text{between}} &= \Sigma n_{\text{group}}(M_{\text{group}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2 \\
&\approx 5(3.53)^2 + 5(0.73)^2 \\
&\quad {}+ 5(-4.27)^2 \\
&\approx 156.13
\end{aligned}
$$

$$ df_{\text{between}} = k - 1 = 3 - 1 = 2 $$

Now for the new component, $SS_{\text{people}}$. @tbl-related-anova-people, a little further down, lists each child's mean under their name, and the People column shows the squared deviation of that mean from the grand mean. Each kid's three rows get the same value, which is why multiplying the one squared deviation by $k$ works. For Stephen, for example:

$$
\begin{gathered}
k(M_{\text{person}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2 \\
= 3(48.00 - 46.67)^2 \approx 5.33
\end{gathered}
$$

Doing the same for each of the other children and adding the five contributions gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_{\text{people}} &= \Sigma k(M_{\text{person}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2 \\
&\approx 5.33 + 75.00 + 56.33 \\
&\quad {}+ 456.33 + 8.33 \\
&\approx 601.33
\end{aligned}
$$

$$ df_{\text{people}} = n - 1 = 5 - 1 = 4 $$

Then we can find $SS_{\text{error}}$ by subtracting $SS_{\text{people}}$ from $SS_{\text{within}}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_{\text{error}} &= SS_{\text{within}} - SS_{\text{people}} \\
&\approx 627.20 - 601.33 \\
&\approx 25.87
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
df_{\text{error}} &= df_{\text{within}} - df_{\text{people}} \\
&= 12 - 4 = 8
\end{aligned}
$$

But let's also see how the error component builds up from the individual scores, starting with one of Stephen's. Remember Stephen's adjusted first-alone time was 49.67 seconds. The first-alone mean stayed at 50.20. So his adjusted score is $49.67 - 50.20 = -0.53$ seconds from that condition's mean. Squaring that deviation gives about 0.28. @tbl-related-anova-people shows both the people squares and these error squares for every score.

+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Child                     | Condition         | Score, $X$ | People: $(M_{\text{person}}-M_{\text{grand}})^2$ | Error: $(X-M_{\text{person}}-M_{\text{group}}+M_{\text{grand}})^2$ |
+===========================+===================+============+==================================================+====================================================================+
| Stephen M.                | First alone       | $51$       | $1.33^2=1.78$                                    | $(-0.53)^2=0.28$                                                   |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           | Second&nbsp;alone | $50$       | $1.33^2=1.78$                                    | $1.27^2=1.60$                                                      |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           | Competition       | $43$       | $1.33^2=1.78$                                    | $(-0.73)^2=0.54$                                                   |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $M_{\text{person}}=48.00$ |                   |            |                                                  |                                                                    |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Mary W.                   | First alone       | $56$       | $5.00^2=25.00$                                   | $0.80^2=0.64$                                                      |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           | Second&nbsp;alone | $53$       | $5.00^2=25.00$                                   | $0.60^2=0.36$                                                      |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           | Competition       | $46$       | $5.00^2=25.00$                                   | $(-1.40)^2=1.96$                                                   |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $M_{\text{person}}=51.67$ |                   |            |                                                  |                                                                    |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Bertha A.                 | First alone       | $56$       | $4.33^2=18.78$                                   | $1.47^2=2.15$                                                      |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           | Second&nbsp;alone | $49$       | $4.33^2=18.78$                                   | $(-2.73)^2=7.47$                                                   |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           | Competition       | $48$       | $4.33^2=18.78$                                   | $1.27^2=1.60$                                                      |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $M_{\text{person}}=51.00$ |                   |            |                                                  |                                                                    |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Clyde G.                  | First alone       | $36$       | $(-12.33)^2=152.11$                              | $(-1.87)^2=3.48$                                                   |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           | Second&nbsp;alone | $35$       | $(-12.33)^2=152.11$                              | $(-0.07)^2=0.00$                                                   |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           | Competition       | $32$       | $(-12.33)^2=152.11$                              | $1.93^2=3.74$                                                      |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $M_{\text{person}}=34.33$ |                   |            |                                                  |                                                                    |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Lucile W.                 | First alone       | $52$       | $1.67^2=2.78$                                    | $0.13^2=0.02$                                                      |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           | Second&nbsp;alone | $50$       | $1.67^2=2.78$                                    | $0.93^2=0.87$                                                      |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           | Competition       | $43$       | $1.67^2=2.78$                                    | $(-1.07)^2=1.14$                                                   |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $M_{\text{person}}=48.33$ |                   |            |                                                  |                                                                    |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| **Sum of squares**        |                   |            | $SS_{\text{people}}=601.33$                      | $SS_{\text{error}}=25.87$                                          |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+

: Each child's three scores, with the two new squared deviations. Values are rounded; the sums use unrounded values. {#tbl-related-anova-people}


With all the sums of squares and degrees of freedom in hand, we can get the two mean squares:

$$
\begin{align}
MS_{\text{between}} &= \frac{SS_{\text{between}}}{df_{\text{between}}} = \frac{156.13}{2} = 78.07 \\
MS_{\text{error}} &= \frac{SS_{\text{error}}}{df_{\text{error}}} = \frac{25.87}{8} = 3.23
\end{align}
$$

Finally, we divide the between-groups mean square by the error mean square:

$$ F = \frac{MS_{\text{between}}}{MS_{\text{error}}} = \frac{78.07}{3.23} \approx 24.14 $$

And here's the completed summary table:

::: {#tbl-related-anova-summary .sfs-summary-table}
| Source | $SS$ | $df$ | $MS$ | $F$ |
|:-------|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Between groups | 156.13 | 2 | 78.07 | 24.14 |
| Within groups | 627.20 | 12 | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |
| &emsp;Between people | 601.33 | 4 | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |
| &emsp;Error | 25.87 | 8 | 3.23 | []{.sfs-na} |
| Total | 783.33 | 14 | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |

Completed related-samples ANOVA summary table for the competition example.
:::

### Step 4: Make a decision

So now we compare our $F$ ratio to the critical value. Our $F$ of $24.14$ is well beyond $4.46$, so we reject the null hypothesis. There is a significant difference among our three conditions. The corresponding $p$-value is about $.0004$, so $p$ is less than $\alpha$.

::: {#fig-related-anova-decision}
{{< interactive-figure relatedAnovaTestDecision makeDistributionGraph options='{"color":"var(--sfs-null-color, currentColor)","distribution":"f","df1":2,"df2":8,"title":"Null distribution: F(2, 8)","style":"minimal","xAxis":true,"yLabel":false,"xDomain":[0,27],"xTicks":6,"labels":{"x":"F ratio"},"shade":{"tail":"right","alpha":0.05},"markers":[{"at":4.45897,"label":"4.46","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-critical-color, #c63f3f)"},{"at":24.14433,"label":"F = 24.14","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-accent, #2c7fb8)"}],"maxWidth":"42rem"}' fallback="Null F distribution with 2 and 8 degrees of freedom. The rejection region lies above 4.46; the observed F of 24.14 is far into the rejection region." >}}

The observed $F = 24.14$ falls beyond the critical value of the null $F$ distribution with $df = 2$ and $8$.
:::

{{< include quizzes/15-related-anova-calculate-f.qmd >}}

### Step 5: Estimate the effect, compare the conditions, and consider power

#### Effect size: partial $\eta^2$

In Chapter 14 we used $\eta^2$, the between-groups sum of squares as a proportion of the total. If you picture all the variability in the data as one big bucket, full to the brim, $\eta^2$ gave the proportion filled by between-groups variability.

For related-samples ANOVA, we use **partial eta squared**, $\eta^2_p$. We take our full bucket and dump out $SS_{\text{people}}$ first, leaving only the between-groups and error components. Then we ask what proportion of the new total is between groups.

More mathematically, the remaining total is $SS_{\text{between}} + SS_{\text{error}}$. That's the same as $SS_{\text{total}} - SS_{\text{people}}$. So:

$$\eta^2_p = \frac{SS_{\text{between}}}{SS_{\text{between}} + SS_{\text{error}}} = \frac{156.13}{156.13 + 25.87} = .86$$

About 86% of that remaining variability is between conditions. Ordinary $\eta^2$ would give $.20$, because it includes the large people component in the denominator.

Why set the people component aside? Because it isn't something our conditions could ever explain. Clyde is fast in every race; no amount of practice or competition accounts for that. And its size depends on which kids we happened to get. If our five kids had all been about as quick as one another, $SS_{\text{people}}$ would have been much smaller, and ordinary $\eta^2$ much bigger, even with exactly the same effect of the conditions. Partial $\eta^2$ isn't swayed by that.

But it does mean partial $\eta^2$ isn't directly comparable to the $\eta^2$ we calculated in Chapter 14. With independent groups, differences between people stay in the denominator, because we have no way of taking them out. So don't line up our .86 next to Chapter 14's .65 and conclude that competition does more for kids than a radioactive spider bite.

#### Post-hoc tests

The ANOVA tells us the population means aren't all equal, but not which ones differ. Remember that Tukey's HSD gives us the minimum difference between means that counts as significant, while controlling the chance of at least one Type I error across all the pairwise comparisons. The idea is exactly the same here.

In Chapter 14, we used $MS_{\text{within}}$ to represent background variability. Here we use $MS_{\text{error}}$, because we've set aside differences in the children's overall speed. It's the same adjustment we made for the $F$ ratio. We also use the error degrees of freedom when looking up the critical $q$.

In @tbl-related-anova-q, find the column for three conditions and the row for $df_{\text{error}} = 8$. Their intersection gives the critical studentized range value, $q = 4.04$, for $\alpha = .05$.

::: {#tbl-related-anova-q}
{{< interactive-figure relatedAnovaTukeyTable makeTukeyTable options='{"title":"Tukey critical values for the competition test","alpha":0.05,"k":{"from":2,"to":6},"df":{"from":4,"to":10},"tableMinWidth":"0","cellMinWidth":"0","maxWidth":"36rem","interactive":false,"selected":{"k":3,"df":8,"alpha":0.05}}' fallback="Studentized range critical values at alpha .05 for 2 through 6 conditions and error df 4 through 10. The highlighted cell for 3 conditions and 8 error degrees of freedom is q = 4.04." >}}

Critical values of $q$ for $\alpha = .05$. The column gives the number of conditions; the row gives the error degrees of freedom.
:::

And $n = 5$, the number of scores in each condition:

$$HSD = q \sqrt{\frac{MS_{\text{error}}}{n}} = 4.04 \sqrt{\frac{3.23}{5}} \approx 3.25$$

So a difference between means greater than 3.25 seconds is significant at the $.05$ level.

| Comparison | Absolute difference | Exceeds 3.25 seconds? |
|:--|--:|:--:|
| First alone vs. second alone | 2.80 seconds | No |
| Second alone vs. competition | 5.00 seconds | Yes |
| First alone vs. competition | 7.80 seconds | Yes |

The two gaps involving competition exceed the HSD, but the gap between the solo trials doesn't. The children improved by an average of 2.80 seconds before competing, and by another 5.00 seconds when competition began.

#### Statistical power

As before, statistical power is the probability of detecting a difference among the population means when there really is one. Accounting for individual differences can help, but a related-samples design doesn't automatically give us more power. The advantage depends on how much the scores go together across conditions.

Think of Clyde again. He's fast in every race, so separating out differences in overall speed removes a lot of the within-groups variability. That can give us a much smaller denominator than we'd get by treating the same scores as independent. (Analyzed as independent samples, these 15 scores give just $F(2, 12) = 1.49$, nowhere near the critical 3.89.) But separating out the people component also costs degrees of freedom, which raises the critical $F$. The reduction in error needs to be enough to compensate. If people's scores in the different conditions weren't related, we'd generally end up with a similar error mean square to the independent-samples analysis, but fewer degrees of freedom and less power. As in Chapter 13, the design tells us which analysis to use; we don't try both and keep whichever gives the result we prefer.

Statistical software can calculate power for a related-samples ANOVA, or work backwards to estimate how many participants we'd need for a target such as 80% power. We need to specify differences worth detecting, estimate the variability and how strongly scores go together across conditions, and choose an alpha level.

## Reporting and interpreting results

So finally, we're ready to report the results. As usual, you need descriptives for each condition; a statement of what test was performed and whether it was significant; the test statistic itself with degrees of freedom; $p$ compared to $\alpha$; and effect size. And here we summarize which post-hoc comparisons were significant and which weren't.

> In this selected five-child example, a single-factor, related-samples ANOVA revealed a significant difference among children's times on their first race alone ($M = 50.20$, $SD = 8.26$ seconds), a second race alone ($M = 47.40$, $SD = 7.09$ seconds), and a race in competition ($M = 42.40$, $SD = 6.19$ seconds); $F(2, 8) = 24.14$, $p < .001$, $\eta^2_p = .86$. Tukey HSD comparisons indicated that children were significantly faster in competition than on either solo trial. The two solo trials did not differ significantly.

What kind of graph would work best to visualize results like these? A simple bar graph showing condition means with confidence intervals wouldn't convey the relatedness of the scores. Really we're interested in how consistently each child's time changed across the conditions, rather than treating the conditions as independent.

@fig-related-profiles emphasizes that. Each colored line follows one child across the races. Every line falls at both steps, even though the children start at quite different levels. Lower times mean faster performances. But the graph leaves out confidence intervals, so the statistical results still need to accompany it.

::: {#fig-related-profiles}
{{< interactive-figure relatedProfileLines makeProfileLines options='{"categories":["First alone","Second alone","Competition"],"series":[{"name":"Stephen","color":0,"values":[51,50,43]},{"name":"Mary W.","color":3,"values":[56,53,46]},{"name":"Bertha","color":7,"values":[56,49,48]},{"name":"Clyde","color":1,"values":[36,35,32]},{"name":"Lucile","color":5,"values":[52,50,43]}],"showMean":true,"yDomain":[30,60],"yLabel":"Time (seconds)","xLabel":"Condition","ariaLabel":"One line per child across the three conditions. Every child’s line falls from first alone to second alone and again to competition. A bold dashed average line falls from 50.20 to 47.40 to 42.40 seconds."}' fallback="One line per child across the three conditions. Every line falls at each step. The bold dashed average line falls from 50.20 to 47.40 to 42.40 seconds." >}}

Times for each child, with a bold dashed line showing the average in each condition.
:::

### Interpreting the results

So what has this analysis told us? At the start of the chapter, I set up the extra solo race as a way of teasing apart practice and competition. So, did we manage it? Not really, no!

The larger improvement when competition began fits the idea that a rival helped the children speed up. But a nonsignificant solo-to-solo comparison doesn't mean practice had no effect. And a significant change after a nonsignificant one doesn't establish that the two changes differ. The question I posed was whether the competition race brought more improvement than practice alone would. That's a comparison between the two *changes*---the 2.80-second drop and the 5.00-second drop---and neither the ANOVA nor Tukey's test makes it. Look at Bertha in @fig-related-profiles: she improved by 7 seconds between her two solo races, then by just 1 second when the rival showed up. (We could test that comparison directly, though it's beyond what we're covering here. With these five kids it wouldn't come close to significance.) The times suggest a story; the tests haven't proved that story.

There's also the order problem. Competition always came third for these kids, so we don't know how fast they would have gone on a third trial alone. Further practice could explain some or all of the improvement we attributed to competition.

So what would a better study look like? First, we'd want to vary the order properly. Triplett went partway there. His two groups of children followed different sequences, but both started with a solo race, so competition never came first. Ideally some kids would compete first, some second, and some third, so that practice was spread evenly across the conditions rather than piling up in one of them.

But that brings its own problem: competing might itself affect a later solo trial. Triplett mentioned that the faster performance some children showed in competition endured into their later alone races, as if the rival unlocked some potential that didn't go away when the competition was over [@triplett1898dynamogenic]. So we might also want more solo races, to map out how much kids improve with practice alone, or a separate group of kids who never compete at all, for comparison. And of course we'd want a lot more than five kids.

Each fix makes the study bigger, longer, and more complicated to analyze, and raises new questions. Every design rules some explanations out and leaves others standing, and part of interpreting results is being clear about which is which.

Lastly, remember that I picked these five children to make a satisfying dataset to work with; they don't reflect trends in Triplett's full dataset. As I mentioned in Chapter 13, modern reanalysis of Triplett's reported data does not establish any conclusive effects of social facilitation.

### Assumptions

The same sort of considerations apply to ANOVA with related samples as in Chapter 14 where we used ANOVA with independent samples. Some slight tweaks are required to accommodate the relatedness of the scores though, much like the assumptions of the related-samples $t$ test.

First, there's the assumption of independence. This only applies within groups. We expect scores from the same child to be related, but different children's responses should be independent of one another.

The assumption of normality likewise concerns the within-person variability we're analyzing, rather than the distribution of raw scores in each condition.

Lastly, remember Chapter 14's homogeneity of variance assumption: we needed comparable variability across groups. Here we have a similar requirement, but it applies to the *difference scores* for every pair of conditions, rather than to the scores within each condition. The requirement is called **sphericity**: the population variances of those difference scores should be the same. (This wasn't an issue with the related-samples $t$ test because with only two conditions, there's just one set of difference scores, so no different variabilities to compare.)

::: {#fig-sphericity}


Sphericity.

:::

In simple terms, sphericity means that we're assuming that people are affected in a roughly consistent way by the different conditions. Imagine that the children improved by about the same amount from their first solo race to their second. The consistency of the differences means that those difference scores would have little variability. But suppose competition helped some children a lot and hindered others. The alone-to-competition difference scores would be much more variable. A single pooled estimate of all that variability wouldn't represent both kinds of change equally well. The *average* changes can differ---a bigger improvement from alone-to-competition versus the first and second alone races, for example. It's the *variability* around those averages that needs to be fairly consistent.

Statistical software can check for unacceptably different variances across the differences and apply a correction. If you see something like "Greenhouse–Geisser" in your output, that's one such correction, which reduces the degrees of freedom to allow for the unequal variability, increasing the critical $F$ required to reject the null to adjust for the violation. Post-hoc tests like Tukey's HSD are also sensitive to sphericity and need to be adjusted if sphericity is questionable.

For our worked example, software would tell you that the sphericity is acceptable, but with so few scores changing one value or adding one more child could change that. As usual, the more data we have, the more reliable not only the estimates of means and things become, but also our assessment of the extent to which assumptions like this are met or violated.
